title: Cap. III Sol.: praedamnation rests on sin foresight; election and damnation not parallel
pass_a_gloss: But if by reprobation the act of praedamning, or of deputing to destruction, is understood, I gladly acknowledge that this divine act rests on foresight of human sin. But then I say that election to glory and deputation to punishment are not of equal reason: For God can destine the undeserving to glory from the mere good pleasure of his will, because he is good, but he cannot destine the undeserving to punishment without intuition of sin, because he is just. Augustine observed this distinction against Julian book 3 chapter 18. God is good, God is just: he can free without good merits, because he is good; he cannot damn without evil merits, because he is just.
pass_b_english: But if reprobation means praedamning — deputing to destruction — I gladly grant that divine act rests on foresight of human sin. Election to glory and deputation to punishment are not on equal footing: God can destine the undeserving to glory from mere good pleasure, because he is good; he cannot destine the undeserving to punishment without intuition of sin, because he is just. Augustine marked that difference (Contra Jul. 3.18): God is good, God is just — he can free without good merits because he is good; he cannot damn without evil merits because he is just.
source_text: Verum si per reprobationem intelligatur actus praedamnandi, sive deputandi ad interitum, lubens agnosco hunc actum Divinum inniti praescientiae peccati humani. Sed tum dico non esse paris rationis electionem ad gloriam, et deputationem ad poenam: Nam Deus potest immerentem destinare ad gloriam ex mero beneplacito voluntatis suae, quia bonus est, sed non potest immerentem destinare ad poenam absque intuitu peccati, quia justus est. Observavit hoc discrimen Augustinus advers. Julian. lib. 3. cap. 18. Bonus est Deus, justus est Deus: potest sine bonis meritis liberare, quia bonus est; non potest sine malis meritis damnare, quia justus est.
